title: Top three scores
topic: A leaderboard helper that passed every single-digit test
blurb: A leaderboard helper that returns the three highest numeric scores.
prompt: Spec: return the three highest numeric scores from `scores` in descending order without mutating the input array. Review this helper — tap a line if it breaks the spec, or let it pass.
conclusion: AI summary: Copies the array, sorts ascending, reverses to descending, and slices the top 3.

diagnosis_choices.label: With no comparator, JS `.sort()` compares numbers as strings — so `'9'` beats `'100'` and high scores drop off.
`.sort()` returns a brand-new array instead of sorting in place, so `copy` stays unsorted.
Calling `.sort()` on a `const` array throws TypeError because `const` prevents mutation.
`.sort()` already sorts numbers from highest to lowest, so line 4 flips them upside down.

fix_choices.label: Pass a numeric comparator: `copy.sort((a, b) => a - b)` (or `b - a` and drop `.reverse()`).
Reassign `copy = copy.sort()` so the sorted array isn't discarded.
Change `const copy` to `let copy` so `.sort()` can mutate it.

flaws.explanation: In JavaScript, `.sort()` with no callback converts elements to strings and sorts alphabetically. So `[2, 10, 9, 100]` becomes `[10, 100, 2, 9]`, and reversed top-3 puts `9` ahead of `100`.
flaws.why_tempting: On single-digit test cases like `[5, 2, 9, 7]`, string order and numeric order match — and Python's `.sort()` really is numeric by default.
flaws.catch_rule: Never call `.sort()` without a comparator on JS numbers; always write `.sort((a, b) => a - b)` or `(a, b) => b - a`.
flaws.hint: Run `[2, 10, 9, 100].sort()` in your head as strings instead of numbers.

diagnosis: If `scores` has fewer than 3 items, calling `topThreeScores` throws RangeError on line 5.
Function doesn't check for `scores` being empty, which makes `.sort()` crash.
Missing default `scores = []` prevents spreading arrays.
Accepting `scores` directly mutates the caller's array even with `[...scores]`.
fix: Guard `if (scores.length < 3) return scores;` at the top.
Default `scores = []` in the parameter list.
Return `null` when `scores` has fewer than 3 elements.
Use `structuredClone(scores)` on line 1.

diagnosis: `[...scores]` is a shallow copy, so `copy.sort()` still reorders the caller's `scores` array.
Using `const copy` freezes the array and makes `copy.sort()` throw TypeError.
Spreading `scores` converts numeric entries into strings, breaking line 3.
`[...scores]` drops duplicate scores like `[9, 9, 7]`.
fix: Change `const copy` to `let copy` so it can be sorted in place.
Use `scores.map(Number)` instead of `[...scores]` to keep numbers.
Use `structuredClone(scores)` because spread still mutates the original.
Use `Array.from(scores)` so duplicates aren't removed.

diagnosis: `copy.reverse()` returns a new array and leaves `copy` ascending, so line 5 returns the three *lowest* scores.
Calling `.reverse()` mutates the original `scores` array passed by the caller.
Reversing after sorting breaks tie order on equal numbers and drops duplicates.
`.reverse()` skips index 0 on even-length arrays.
fix: Capture the return value: `const desc = copy.reverse();`.
Drop `.reverse()` and slice from the end with `copy.slice(-3)`.
Clone again before reversing: `[...copy].reverse()`.
Sort descending directly and keep `.reverse()` as a fallback.

diagnosis: `copy.slice(0, 3)` is off by one and returns 4 elements (indices `0, 1, 2, 3`).
When `scores` has only 2 items, `slice(0, 3)` pads the third slot with `undefined`.
`slice(0, 3)` mutates `copy` and returns the removed elements instead of the top three.
`slice(0, 3)` skips index 0 and returns indices `1, 2, 3`.
fix: Change to `copy.slice(0, 2)` so only 3 elements are returned.
Guard `copy.slice(0, Math.min(3, copy.length))` so short arrays don't get `undefined`.
Replace `slice(0, 3)` with `splice(0, 3)` so it doesn't pad.
Use `copy.slice(1, 4)` to grab the first three slots.

diagnosis: Missing semicolon after the function causes strict-mode syntax errors.
`copy` isn't cleared before returning, leaking memory across calls.
Closing brace ends the function before `copy.reverse()` finishes.
Should export `topThreeScores` or callers can't pass arrays.
fix: Add `};` at the end of the function.
Add `copy.length = 0;` after slicing.
Wrap the function in `export function topThreeScores(scores)`.
Return a `Set` so the top three are always unique.

clean_conclusion: In JS, `.sort()` without a comparator turns numbers into strings — `'9'` beats `'100'`. Passing `(a, b) => a - b` (or `b - a`) actually sorts by value.
